Many measurements strike me as more convincing than reliable.

I first began thinking about this while studying cardiac troponin, the biomarker used in emergency care to help diagnose a heart attack. The paradox is that it also rises in healthy athletes after a race or a match. The same molecule. The same increase. And two incompatible meanings.

I devoted my doctoral thesis to understanding this paradox. But what I really took from it was a question that still guides everything I do: how do we measure what exercise does to the body, why do we measure it that way, and, above all, what can we claim from what we have measured?

Since then, I have been as interested in what we measure as in how we measure it. Instruments always return a number. The difficult part is deciding whether that number deserves the confidence we tend to place in it.

That is where my fascination with statistics comes from: not only as a tool for analysing data, but as a way of thinking about what we know, what we do not know, and how certain we can be about a claim. It is also why I teach research methods at master's level and spend much of my time collaborating on projects far removed from my own.

I currently lead EXCURSE (2025–2028), a project examining how muscle excursion range during strength training shapes adaptation. We compare training across different regions of the muscle's excursion range to study changes in muscle architecture, strength, neuromuscular activation, and mechanical properties. We want to know whether describing exercise from the perspective of the muscle—not only through joint motion—allows us to understand training adaptations more clearly.

I am an Associate Professor of Kinesiology at INEFC Lleida and, since 2022, I have coordinated the centre's research support. My work combines exercise physiology, biomechanics, and methodology, but almost all of it ultimately revolves around the same idea: how much confidence can we place in a measurement?
